title: .NET 10 and C# 14
sub: What is actually new and what has been around for years
cards/0/body:
The headline of every recent release is speed. The JIT removes more memory allocations and virtual calls, and libraries get Span<T>-based APIs that avoid extra copies.

And there is a new language version: C# 14.
cards/1/title: Not new, though people often think so
cards/1/body:
Nullable references: C# 8 (2019). On by default in project templates since .NET 6.
Records: C# 9 (2020).
Span<T>: 2018 (.NET Core 2.1 and C# 7.2).

None of these arrived in .NET 10. They just got easier to use and spread wider through the libraries.
cards/2/q: Match each feature to the C# version that introduced it
cards/3/body: Adding logic to a setter used to mean declaring a backing field by hand. Now field is the hidden backing field of an auto-property.
cards/4/body:
An extension block adds not just methods but also properties to someone else's type.

Assignment through ?.: if the left side is null, nothing happens.
cards/5/q: A property that trims spaces, with no field of your own
cards/5/explain: _name would work only if you declared that field yourself.
cards/6/body: In .NET 10 you can run a one-file program with no project: dotnet run app.cs. Packages are pulled in by a directive right in the file. Handy for scripts and experiments.
cards/7/q: What does customer?.Order = GetOrder() do when customer is null?
cards/7/options/0: Nothing: no assignment happens, and GetOrder() is not called
cards/7/explain: The right side is evaluated only if the left side is not null.
cards/8/q: What is actually new in C# 14 / .NET 10? Select all that apply.
cards/8/explain: Records and nullable are old features, from C# 9 and C# 8.
cards/9/q: Where do you usually see the biggest win from moving to a new .NET without changing code?
cards/9/options/0: Speed: the JIT and libraries get faster with every release
cards/9/explain: Many teams see a gain just by switching the target and rebuilding.
